ideas.title: Blow glass: breath, heat and gravity shape the bubble
ideas.critique: This answers round 2's solver worry: a Maxwell shell whose rest shape relaxes at E/eta, run on code that already exists, with per-triangle volume giving the thickness and a closed-form sphere test, is a model that can actually be built and checked. A glowing bubble that sags and stiffens as it cools is new physics with a skill to it, and traced emission turning into a clear dielectric of the real thickness is a good subject. Without remeshing, a big swell will stretch triangles until the burst rule follows the mesh, not the glass. The film of one object up close is the island's usual shot, and what is left at the end is one more vessel-shaped prop.

ideas.title: A sandcastle against the tide
ideas.nearest: A snowball that grows as it rolls, a take that misses
ideas.critique: Breaking it into stages with numbers to pass (an angle of repose, a vertical wall that stands) makes the round 2 idea honest: stage 1 alone is new physics the island has never had, and dry sand sliding into a cone beside a damp tower that stands is a clear film. The play only arrives in stages 2 and 3, though. This session's film shows two piles of sand and no game yet, and a 2 m box of MPM grains is far smaller than a beach a player can build on live.

ideas.title: Dig a stream: water carves where you scratched
ideas.critique: Virtual-pipe shallow water with a capacity-law erosion model is the standard method for terrain erosion in games and demos, so the physics is well known even if the island never had it. A scratch that grows into a river with bends and a fan is the same 'a path you started wears itself into the ground' payoff as the ants' trail. What is strong is that it is play right away: scratch, dam with stones, watch the water go round, all in one session. Water that carves the meadow live is something people come back to.
